newsitem.title: USA: Abortion hearing aimed at 'truth' raises hackles.
newsitem.headline: Abortion hearing aimed at 'truth' raises hackles.

text.p: Open hostility reigned Tuesday at a Capitol Hill hearing into what opponents call partial-birth abortion, six days after a controversial bill to ban the procedure was re-introduced.

The lines were clearly drawn at the start of a standing-room-only joint hearing of the Senate and House judiciary panels, with abortion rights proponents faulting the proposed ban as unconstitutional and abortion foes calling the procedure itself barbaric.

"The debate is so politicized you have forgotten we are real people serving real people," Renee Chelian, president of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, testified. "The truth is no surgery is pretty or easy to describe. If looking at graphic photos or diagrams of heart bypass or organ transplant made you queasy, would you vote to ban them?"

Chelian's comments were aimed directly at abortion opponents' contention that so-called partial birth abortion, sometimes known as intact dilation and extraction, is a gruesome procedure akin to infanticide.
The procedure involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

The issue has sparked heated debate since a ban was first introduced in Congress in 1995 but vetoed last year by President Bill Clinton, who has said he would sign a bill that provided exceptions for cases where the woman's life or health was at stake. The current bill, like the former one, allows only for cases where the woman's life is in jeopardy.

For more than four hours, four witnesses who favoured abortion rights sparred with two who opposed them, and the whole proceding began with the airing of a public television examination contending that the news media had generally failed to fairly report about the procedure.
Notably absent from the hearing was Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of Chelian's group, who caused a furore two weeks ago by saying he lied when he defended the procedure.
Instead of the 500 or so a year cited by abortion rights advocates, he said as many as 5,000 might be performed, many on women in earlier stages of non-crisis pregnancies.

The joint congressional hearing, entitled "Partial Birth Abortion: The Truth," featured repeated interruptions of witness testimony by other witnesses and by members of Congress, some of whom had just returned from a retreat to encourage more civility.

At one point, abortion opponent Douglas Johnson of the National Right to Life Committee pulled from his briefcase a pink plastic model of what he said was a foetus at 20 weeks gestation, as well as a pair of surgical scissors said to be used in the procedure.

Representative Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican who has consistently opposed abortion, wrangled with witness Gloria Feldt, president of Planned Parenthood Federation of America, saying she was unnerved by this particular abortion procedure "because you can't avoid the foetus, babies four-fifths born."
Feldt responded, "Please don't say to me that I don't care about the foetus and please don't say to me that none of us involved in the reproductive rights movement care about the foetus."

A second panel of witnesses featured testimony from three women who were given disastrous prognoses for their pregnancies. Two of the women described in emotional detail how they decided to have the controversial abortion procedure, while a third attended the hearing with her toddler son, whom she chose to bear despite predictions of severe anomalies.

Dr. Curtis Cook, a specialist in high-risk pregnancies, testified that some women's ability to carry a subsequent pregnancy to term might be compromised after having a so-called partial birth abortion.
